nameStory: This tiny hummingbird is named after Calliope, the ancient Greek muse of epic poetry and eloquence. Just as the muse inspired beautiful words, this little bird seems to inspire wonder with its jewel-like throat feathers that shimmer like tiny gems. The name perfectly captures the magical quality of encountering North America's smallest bird.
description: The Calliope Hummingbird is North America's tiniest bird, about the size of a large bee or small butterfly. Males sport brilliant magenta-purple streaks on their white throats that look like rays of colored light, while females have peachy-buff sides and spotted throats. These western wanderers are incredibly rare visitors to New England, with only three recorded sightings in the region. Despite their small size, they're mighty migrants, traveling thousands of miles twice a year between their western breeding grounds and southern wintering areas.

idTips.label: Gorget pattern
idTips.description: Males have distinctive magenta-purple streaks radiating from a white throat base, looking like colorful whiskers or rays of light rather than a solid throat patch

idTips.label: Size comparison
idTips.description: Noticeably smaller than other hummingbirds - about the size of your thumb from tip to wrist, making even Ruby-throats look large by comparison

idTips.label: Tail shape
idTips.description: Short, rounded tail that doesn't extend past the wingtips when perched, giving a compact, stubby appearance

idTips.label: Female coloring
idTips.description: Females show warm peachy-buff wash on the sides and flanks, with small dark spots scattered across a whitish throat

idTips.label: Flight sound
idTips.description: Wings produce a higher-pitched buzz than larger hummingbirds, almost like a large bumblebee's hum

habitat: Since Calliope Hummingbirds are extremely rare vagrants to New England, they could theoretically appear anywhere with flowers or feeders. In their normal western range, they prefer mountain meadows and forest edges, so any New England sighting would likely be at hummingbird feeders in yards, gardens, or parks during migration periods.

seasonality.spring: Extremely unlikely to appear, but any vagrant would most likely show up at feeders during late spring migration in May.
seasonality.summer: Virtually no chance of occurrence, as they breed in western mountains thousands of miles away.
seasonality.fall: Slightly more possible than spring, with any vagrant likely appearing at feeders during August or September migration.
seasonality.winter: No chance of occurrence, as they winter in Mexico and Central America.

funFact: Despite being North America's smallest bird, weighing less than a penny, the Calliope Hummingbird completes one of the longest migrations relative to body size of any bird on Earth - that's like a human walking around the entire planet twice each year!
confusionNotes: In New England, the streaky throat pattern could potentially be confused with a young male Ruby-throated Hummingbird developing its gorget, but Calliopers are noticeably smaller and have the distinctive radiating magenta streaks rather than scattered red spots.
contextualKnowledge: The Calliope Hummingbird was once placed in its own genus called Stellula, meaning 'little star,' which beautifully described both its tiny size and sparkling appearance. Recent genetic research moved it into the Selasphorus genus with other western hummingbirds, showing how DNA studies sometimes reshape our understanding of bird relationships.
compareHints: Compared to its Selasphorus relatives like Rufous and Allen's Hummingbirds, the Calliope is much smaller and males have the unique streaky throat pattern instead of solid-colored gorgets. The Rufous Hummingbird is larger with extensive orange-red coloring, while Allen's has a solid red-orange gorget and is also significantly larger than the tiny Calliope.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Unlike its close relatives, the rufous hummingbird is the only Selasphorus species regularly recorded in New England, making identification easier.
Allen's Hummingbird is nearly identical to the Rufous Hummingbird, with males showing slightly more orange tones in their throat patches versus the Rufous's more intense red-orange.

Compared to its close relative the Rufous Hummingbird (another western species), male Broad-tailed Hummingbirds have rose-red rather than orange-red throats and lack the extensive rufous coloring on the back and sides.
